newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya to limit official contacts with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya to limit official contacts with Russia.

text.p: Chechnya's president has suspended his ministers' talks with Moscow in a bid to speed up the release of Russian funds, but will maintain top-level contacts, Interfax news agency said on Tuesday.

"President Aslan Maskhadov has banned all ministers' trips to Moscow and all talks with Russian officials until a plan to rebuild Chechnya is signed," Maskhadov's spokesman Kazbek Khadzhiyev told Reuters in Grozny, capital of the breakaway Russian region.

He later told Interfax that the halt did not mean a blanket ban on negotiations with the Kremlin, which the Chechens see as vital for preserving peace after 21 months of war which claimed tens of thousands of lives. The limits on contacts were designed, rather, to concentrate attention on the need for cash.
"We attribute special importance to dialogue with Russia and we are not going to stop it," Khadzhiyev was quoted as saying.
First deputy premier Movladi Udugov will head to Moscow in the next couple of weeks for talks with Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council.
"The president (Maskhadov) deems it necessary to offer to Moscow a complex plan of reconstructing Chechnya's companies and social infrastructure," Khadzhiyev told Interfax.

"Separate ageements betweeen Moscow and Grozny on the ministerial level do not help to speed up the reconstruction of Chechnya's devastated towns and villages," he added referring to a flow of deals struck recently in many different fields.

The halt to talks at ministerial level might, however, delay negotiations on renovating a pipeline through which early oil from new Azeri offshore fields is set to flow to world markets through Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk this autumn.

Chechen leaders, who signed a ceasefire with Moscow last August after ousting Russian troops from Grozny, insist that their Moslem southern region is independent from Russia. Under a peace pact, the question of formal sovereignty was set aside.
As a part of the peace deal the Kremlin pledged to plough in funds to rebuild its economy and infrastructure.

Though never spelled out, many analysts see the promise of funds as a quid pro quo for the Chechens dropping demands for recognition of their sovereignty. Maskhadov, seen as a moderate in Moscow, won a presidential election in January.

In a sign of improving relations, Russian and Chechen officials signed a deal earlier this month detailing how they would repair the war-damaged pipeline that runs across Chechnya. But many aspects of the accord remain unsettled.

The issue is crucial for the two sides and they are interested in solving the problem as soon as possible, as the oil is expected to provide both Russia and Chechnya with generous revenues in transport fees.

Interfax news agency said Maskhadov on Monday met the Grozny representative of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and complained Moscow was not fulfilling economic treaties signed earlier.
He also asked the OSCE for broader aid to Chechnya.
Interfax quoted Rybkin as saying Moscow and the Chechen authorities had never stopped working on rebuilding Chechnya's economy "and never would stop, not even for a minute".
He did not say, however, when he expected the concrete reconstruction plan to be approved and the work to start.
